analysis.one_liner: Requires large private companies to publicly disclose their finances like public companies do.
analysis.headline: The Senate Banking Committee held a hearing on the bill but never voted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require very large private companies — those worth more than $700 million, or with more than $5 billion in revenue and 5,000 employees — to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission and file public financial reports, just as public companies must [S2]. Today, companies can stay private indefinitely and keep their finances, debts, and valuation secret from investors, employees, and the public [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced by Senator Jack Reed with two Democratic cosponsors, got one hearing, and never received a vote [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday investors — including people whose retirement savings sit in mutual funds — would gain visibility into large private companies whose true finances are currently hidden, making it easier to value public competitors and to know what private funds they may be exposed to. Employees and contractors at large private companies would see the real financial condition of their employers. Small public companies would compete on a more level field, since private giants could no longer keep their books sealed while public rivals must disclose.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirement savers, employees of large private firms

how_it_helps.text: Requires private companies valued above $700 million, or with over $5 billion in revenue and at least 5,000 employees, to register with the SEC and file the same public periodic reports required of public companies.
Counts independent contractors as employees for the size test, so large gig-economy and staffing-heavy private firms cannot avoid disclosure by structuring their workforce as contractors.
Lets the SEC tailor what information the new registrants must file and set transition rules, so the burden can be proportionate rather than one-size-fits-all.

analysis.who_pays: Large private companies — many backed by private equity and venture capital — would bear the cost of SEC registration, annual certifications of their valuation, and public reporting of their financials [S2][S3]. Their owners, executives, and fund investors would lose the ability to shop the company or raise money based on private, unaudited claims about its performance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large private companies and their investors

drawbacks.text: Registration and public reporting are real compliance costs; a company crossing the thresholds would have to build audit, disclosure, and certification functions it never needed while private, and the bill gives the SEC discretion to set exit rules only for some registrants (a valuation-based registrant can deregister only if its valuation falls below $250 million).

Critics of disclosure mandates argue they can push companies to stay smaller, delay hiring, or list abroad rather than cross the thresholds — costs that could fall partly on the workers those companies employ.

The bill's employee definition sweeps in independent contractors, which captures the intended gig-economy targets but also pulls in some staffing-heavy businesses that are not conventional 'unicorn' startups.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and the costs are narrow: public reporting by a few hundred very large private companies would give investors, employees, and competitors real information, while the compliance burden falls only on firms large enough to afford it. The main honest objection is that disclosure requirements may change how some companies grow or structure themselves, and the bill's contractor-counting rule reaches beyond startups. On balance, the transparency gain outweighs a compliance cost imposed on firms with valuations in the hundreds of millions or billions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Banking Committee for the rest of the Congress — it got one hearing in December 2022 but the committee never voted on it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on September 15, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
Senators Catherine Cortez Masto and Elizabeth Warren signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors, both Democrats.
The Banking Committee held a hearing on the bill on December 14, 2022, printed as S.Hrg. 117-757, but took no further action.
The committee never voted to report the bill and the full Senate never considered it; when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large private companies and the private equity and venture capital investors behind them are better off, because they keep the ability to stay private and keep their financials sealed from investors, employees, and competitors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large private companies and their private backers

for.name: Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it at introduction; it was referred to the Banking Committee he serves on.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Sherrod Brown, D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing but never brought the bill to a committee vote, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: Private equity and venture capital industry
against.role: Private-markets investors whose portfolio companies the bill would cover
against.what_they_did: The industry has broadly resisted public-disclosure mandates for private markets, where secrecy about valuations and performance is a core selling point to its own investors.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all three supporters were Democrats, and the bill ended in a committee controlled by Democrats, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Private equity and venture capital firms
industries.note: Their portfolio companies above the thresholds would have to file public financial reports, ending the practice of raising capital and marking valuations based on private, undisclosed numbers. Investors and retirement savers would see what these funds actually own and how those holdings perform.

Companies worth over $700 million or with $5 billion in revenue and 5,000 employees would lose the ability to stay private while keeping their finances secret; they would owe the SEC annual certifications and public reports. Employees and counterparties would finally see the firm's real condition.
Public companies already bear the cost of SEC disclosure; requiring their large private competitors to disclose levels the playing field in competing for capital, customers, and talent.
